body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Audit and feedback: effects on professional practice and healthcare outcomes, an updated systematic review","authors":"Ivarsson-Moore N, Adewale-Grimm K, Tanaka-Holbrook E, Perez-Lindqvist S","year":2017,"venue":"Implementation Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ier.2017.0140","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We updated a systematic review of randomised trials of audit and feedback directed at health professionals. We included 146 trials. The median absolute improvement in compliance with desired practice was 4.3 percentage points (interquartile range 0.5 to 16). Effects were larger when baseline performance was low, when feedback was given more than once, when it was delivered by a supervisor or colleague, and when it included explicit targets and an action plan. Few trials reported patient outcomes or unintended effects, and the design of the feedback itself was rarely described in enough detail to reproduce."},{"title":"Actionable patient lists in primary care dashboards: a controlled before-after study of overdue monitoring","authors":"Mahlangu-Frost D, Okeke-Sandberg R","year":2020,"venue":"Primary Care Quality Reports","doi":"10.5555/pcqr.2020.0266","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared 12 general practices that received a dashboard with a printable list of patients overdue for chronic disease monitoring with 12 practices that received the same dashboard without the list. Over nine months, the proportion of patients up to date with monitoring rose by 9 percentage points in practices given the list and by 2 percentage points in comparison practices. Practices with a recall clerk used the list most. Allocation was by practice preference, and baseline performance was higher in the comparison practices."},{"title":"Peer comparison feedback to general practices: a cluster randomised trial of prescribing and monitoring indicators","authors":"Hollander-Achebe T, Watts-Nakamura J, Silva-Brennan P","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Primary Care Improvement","doi":"10.5555/jpci.2022.0198","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 146 general practices to quarterly feedback that compared each practice with its peers or to usual feedback without comparison. After 12 months, peer comparison increased completion of recommended monitoring by 3.1 percentage points (95 percent confidence interval 0.9 to 5.3). The effect was concentrated in practices in the lowest third of baseline performance. There was no change in prescribing indicators. Practice staff reported that comparisons with dissimilar practices felt unfair. Practices in the highest third of baseline performance showed no change, and a few practices stopped reading the reports after the second quarter."},{"title":"Dashboard use declines after launch: usage log analysis in 58 general practices","authors":"Koenig-Mensah A, Rahman-Olsen D","year":2019,"venue":"Health Informatics in Practice","doi":"10.5555/hip.2019.0053","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed dashboard usage logs from 58 general practices for 18 months after a performance dashboard was launched. Log-ins fell by 71 percent within three months of launch. Practices that assigned the dashboard to a named staff member kept using it. Views of patient-level lists were strongly associated with later improvement in the indicators, while views of summary charts were not. Usage logs cannot show what staff did after viewing the dashboard. Practices without a named owner stopped opening the dashboard within weeks, and few staff in any practice used the summary charts."},{"title":"Kidney testing in type 2 diabetes: test ordered versus test completed in primary care records","authors":"Petrossian-Oduya L, Grant-Varela H","year":2024,"venue":"Diabetes Care in Practice","doi":"10.5555/dcip.2024.0087","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined primary care records of 6,420 people with type 2 diabetes to compare kidney tests ordered with tests completed. In total, 18 percent of ordered urine albumin tests were not completed within three months, compared with 6 percent of ordered eGFR tests. Non-completion was highest among people of working age and those living in the most deprived areas. Indicators based on tests ordered would overstate adherence to the screening guideline. Most uncompleted urine tests had been ordered at a routine review and needed the patient to return a sample later."},{"title":"Overtesting after feedback: duplicate kidney function tests in patients also monitored by hospital clinics","authors":"Lindahl-Owusu C, Farrow-Tanaka M","year":2016,"venue":"Laboratory Use Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After a practice feedback programme on diabetes monitoring, we looked for duplicate testing among 3,115 patients who were also seen in hospital renal or diabetes clinics. In the six months after feedback began, 11 percent had a kidney function test in primary care within 30 days of a hospital test, compared with 5 percent in the six months before. Duplicate tests were rarely acted on. Practices could not see hospital results in their own records, which the authors identify as the cause."},{"title":"Staggered rollout as a natural experiment for evaluating practice-level interventions: methods guidance","authors":"Network Evaluation Methods Group","year":2025,"venue":"Health Services Methods Notes","doi":"10.5555/hsmn.2025.0012","providerType":"report","abstract":"This guidance describes how to evaluate an intervention introduced to groups of practices at different times for administrative reasons. When the timing is set by an external schedule, practices that start later can serve as concurrent comparisons, provided the schedule is not related to performance. The guidance recommends adjusting for baseline performance, checking pre-rollout trends, and analysing at the level of the patient with practice as a random effect. It warns that small numbers of practices give imprecise estimates and that spillover between practices sharing staff can dilute differences."}]}
